Speech:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), I want first to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for the outstanding record he has in this area. I have had the privilege of working with the Member as a member of the Justice Committee for the last five years. I know that before that time, my colleague, the former Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, the former justice critic for my Party, Stuart Leggatt, worked very closely with the Hon. Member for Oxford and always spoke very highly of him.
In his capacity as justice critic, Mr. Leggatt had an opportunity to serve on the subcommittee on penitentiaries, which has already been referred to by the Hon. Member for Oxford. I think it is important in addressing the substance of the motion today that we examine the content of that subcommittee report and also look at what has happened to the report since it was tabled in 1977.
That report arose from the work of the unanimous and non-partisan work of a group of Members of Parliament who were appointed to look into conditions in the Canadian penitentiary system because of some very serious incidents of violence in the system. These incidents occurred in a variety of areas whether Kingston, Laval or other areas. The subcommittee found that the penitentiary system was in a state of crisis at the time they reported. The sub-committee said that unless its recommendations were acted upon and acted upon urgently, that state of crisis would continue.
1 think the Member for Oxford has clearly documented the fact that unfortunately a succession of Solicitors General did not act upon those fundamental recommendations. I will mention Attorneys General as well. I refer to Attorneys General because surely one of the most fundamental recommendations made by that subcommittee was a recommendation that first and foremost in the Canadian criminal justice system we must look at alternatives to imprisonment. That recommendation has been shown to be so very true. The recommendation which that committee made six or seven years ago has been clearly brought out by the experience we have seen since that time. I deeply regret that governments, and I must say governments both Liberal and Conservative, have failed to respond to that very fundamental recommendation.
If we are going to be serious about reform of the criminal justice system and reform of the penal system, we must recognize that our prisons are far too crowded. There are
Maximum Security Prison
literally thousands of people in the Canadian prison system. Instead of serving time behind walls, they should be repaying their debt to society in other non-custodial ways. There are many reasons for that. One can look solely at it from an economic perspective and note that last year the statistics show that in the most recent year for which there were comprehensive statistics, that is 1980 to 1981, governments collectively spent some S845 million on the delivery of adult correctional services.
What is the comparative cost of imprisonment as opposed to non-custodial forms of supervision, community supervision, for example? The per capita cost to Canadians was nine times as high for imprisonment as it was for non-custodial forms of supervision. These alternatives to imprisonment could include fine options, fines geared to income, and community work service. Instead of the community being required to pay some $40,000 to $50,000 per year to incarcerate an individual, he is repaying his debt to society. It can include restitution to the victim of the crime.
There are a variety of other options to imprisonment. We have seen in the country partly as a result of the mandatory 25-year provisions, the compromise made at the time of the debate on capital punishment, prisons which are rapidly becoming overcrowded institutions; indeed, they already are far too crowded. We will have to come to grips with the reality that 25-year minimum sentences will have to be re-examined. If they are not, I predict that we will see serious problems in the very near future.
Overcrowding has a devastating impact on the prison system. We have already looked at the implications of double-bunking within the prison system. We have seen a dramatic rise in violence within the prison system over the last couple of years, whether it be suicides, violence by prisoner against prisoner or indeed violence by prisoner against guard. We have seen the tragedy of Archambault where a number of guards were killed. The level of that violence will surely increase unless we in this Parliament come to grips with the fact that the prison system in Canada has failed.
In the future, in 10 or 20 or 30 years, Canadians will look back on the prison system as one of the most dramatic failures in the criminal justice system. We will ask ourselves as citizens how it was that we could possibly tolerate a system which so demonstrably failed to meet its objectives. We know all too well that there is no serious attempt to rehabilitate in many institutions.
Another critical recommendation of the subcommittee was that there should be meaningful opportunities for work in institutions. I believe a national prison industries program was suggested. That recommendation has not been implemented by a succession of governments. Instead of incarcerating people for lengthy terms without any possibility of rehabilitation, we should be looking at the opportunity for meaningful and effective work for people who are in fact imprisoned.

This nation is seriously in debt, Mr. Speaker. Business confidence has ebbed. Foreign investors have been scared off and unemployment is painfully high. As soon as the election was called, everyone knew what was going to happen. People did not have to wait. People knew the Liberal govern-

ment was going to be turfed out. In the third quarter, we had a dramatic 8 per cent increase in our GNP. Just the fact that the election was called inspired confidence in a new government that everyone knew was going to be elected.
The Government can neither wish nor legislate economic growth and meaningful job opportunities into being. The way must be made clear for the private sector to become confident, to flourish, to invest, and thus to create jobs. The Government must move step by step to remove a wide range of obstacles to growth and new jobs. The private sector must be provided with a stable and comprehensive policy environment. The first order of business is to take action on the deficit. The mounting federal debt has become the single most powerful obstacle to growth and private sector job creation. It has been said that the greatest financial invention was compound interest. From an investment point of view, this may be true, but there is another side to compound interest, that seen by the debtor. The federal Government, unfortunately, has fallen into massive indebtedness that now feeds on itself. New interest charges generate new borrowings, which lead to more and more interest charges, an accelerating treadmill of debt.
Even with relatively favourable assumptions about interest rates and continuing economic growth, the deficit in future years was projected to remain in the range of $34 to $38 billion. On the one hand it was clear that we would not just grow our way out of the deficit problem. We could not spend our way out. In fact, we would be getting into an even greater debt problem unless we took action. The public debt, if left unchecked, would reach a staggering total of $410 billion by the end of this decade, the equivalent of $54,000 for every Canadian family. Each year we are borrowing more and more money just to pay the interest on past debts. In so doing, we are imposing a crippling tax burden on future generations.
When, as is currently the case, more than $1 out of every $3 of tax revenue is used to pay the interest on the national debt, then it is clear we are not only compounding past debts, we are compromising the future. The accumulating debt threatens the creation of permanent jobs for unemployed Canadians today and for our children in the years to come, and it does so in a number of different ways. It puts upward pressure on interest rates by raising the expectations of future inflation and by competing for private savings. It limits the Government's ability to meet priority economic and social needs. It symbolizes a state of economic mismanagement that undermines confidence and threatens the job-creating private investment that Canada needs.
That is why, despite the limited time available, the Government had to make a number of tough decisions which were announced on November 8 as part of the economic statement, decisions to reduce expenditures and to increase revenue recovery as a first step in controlling the deficit. December 3, 1984

I hope I will be forgiven, since this is my first opportunity to say something about Guelph, if I inform this House of some of the background of my community. Such background will help Hon. Members understand the position I take on this and many other issues. Guelph is the county seat for Wellington. It began as an agricultural centre and, I am delighted to say, Mr. Speaker, that it retains much of that soundness and common sense today. Guelph is surrounded by an agricultural area and has a diversity which is envied by most people. It has a sense of history and is a place of beauty. We even have a correctional institution to house those people who come from other parts of the province. We also have a university which has been actively involved in this particular issue. Our university was the site of one of the main peace and disarmament conferences over the past 12 months.
I believe the people of Canada want an end to nuclear weapons. They want peace and they want disarmament. However, the natural caution of most Canadians dictates that we do not want a freeze which has the possibility of harming our strategic position.
I would like to address one specific element in this discussion, namely, verification. In an era of suspicion and uncertainty, nations are unlikely to accede to agreements affecting their own national security without some adequate means of assurance that other signatories will indeed live up to the terms of their agreement. An arms control agreement is essentially an agreement between states to undertake restrictive measures. Since the benefit to each state arises from the compliance of the other, there is, of course, mutual advantage. In simple terms, Mr. Speaker, verification is the means by which such assurance is given to the other states. Consequently, the nature of the verification measures associated with the arms control agreements is of vital importance. The Swedish-Mexican freeze resolution, unlike the other two freeze resolutions at the United Nations, does address the problem of verification in greater detail. The resolution calls for appropriate measures and procedures of verifications such as those which have already been agreed to by the Parties in principle in SALT I and SALT II.
Ignoring the fact, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution is declaratory and thus does not envisage the necessary negotiations of verification measures, there are elements called for in the resolution which simply are not verifiable under the suggested verification procedure. The SALT I and SALT II agreements deal with anti-ballistics missile systems with intercontinental ballistic missiles and with heavy bombers. It is relatively easy to verify the deployment or testing of these major weapons systems by national technical means. Indeed, non-intrusive national technical means are generally adequate to monitor fixed ICBM sites, the number and locations of heavy bombers and the number of submarines actually
Supply
deployed. However, these methods are totally inadequate to monitor tactical nuclear weapons systems or dual use weapons delivery systems which we have today.
Furthermore, countries must still come to grips with how to verify submarine launch Cruise missiles and Cruise missiles which are deployed on surface ships. Stronger verification methods will be needed in order to ensure a ban on deployment and production of nuclear weapons and delivery systems.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am a little perplexed by the fact that none of the Government's supporters are interested in speaking on this debate. I would have hoped that, given the vital importance of the topic we now have before us, it would have generated a little more interest than apparently has been generated to this point in time. I say this recognizing that there are months ahead of us and that there will be ample opportunity by the end of March or early April for anyone who wishes to participate to do so. I do urge upon government back-benchers to remember, however, that the opportunity to give 20-minute speeches will, of course, run out and they will be restricted to making 10-minute comments come the end of February and into early March.
Having said that, I want to say that I doubt very much if, in the life of this Parliament, there will be another debate that will so clearly distinguish the policy direction of the Government from that which would be taken by the New Democratic Party.
I believe it is fair to say that in this debate alone there is a choice to be made. You can either believe with a sort of blind faith that an investor invests out of the goodness of his or her heart, taking into account all of the ramifications and consequences of that investment on other than themselves; or you can believe that an investor with a vested interest-which, of course, ties the two words together-invests in his own best interests and will pay only-cursory attention to the effect of his particular enterprise on those who might come into contact with it or be affected by it. I want to make it clear that I am not saying that investors do not care what happens to other people. 1 am sure they do on an individual basis. I am sure they do not like to see the kind of thing which has just occurred in India where thousands of people were killed or maimed or will suffer for the rest of their lives as a result of inadequate provisions for the protection not only of the workers inside the plant but of the community. I do not believe for one moment that the principals in that particular company consciously sat down and said, "We don't care what happens to those people". But what they did not do, and what they were not required to do, is to make that one of their primary considerations. They were not required to sit down and consciously factor into their costs the cost of providing the kind of environmental and human protection which would have guaranteed that such an occurrence could not take place.
I do not want to attribute to those people all of the worst possible motives. I attribute to them the motives which drive
them, that is, the desire to accumulate wealth. I personally do not share that desire, but I do understand that that goal drives a large number of people in our society and, in fact, it will be held by this Government and by others, not necessarily part of the governing party, as being a worth-while motive.
When one recognizes that that is the primary driving force behind the investor and those who make the decisions on behalf of investors, then one must put in place measures which will guarantee a level of behaviour by those persons which will be satisfactory to the community as a whole. It is interesting to note that investors put those kinds of measures in place to protect themselves from each other, to protect themselves in the stock-market from dealings which would perhaps otherwise result in actions which might be detrimental to the total investment community. What we are suggesting, following along on that example, is the necessity for Members of Parliament and for the Government of Canada to recognize what it is that motivates investors and to then make sure that we have in place the kinds of guarantees which will ensure that the public interest is also served by the investment which takes place.
I would like to say to the Government, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to lose investment dollars to another part of the world simply because that country is prepared to run risks with health, safety or the environment and it is not prepared to take into account the public good, so be it. If a company decides to move from Hamilton to Mexico-as did Allen Industries Canada Ltd.-because of the fact that it can get away with paying pitiful wages, it can get away without protecting the environment, it can get away without industrial accident protection, it does not have to pay unemployment insurance premiums and does not have to provide the benefits that the people of Canada have not only become accustomed to, but deserve, so be it. If an investor is prepared to invest his money elsewhere because he does not have to make those kinds of commitments to Canadians, he can bloody well invest his money elsewhere! That is fine with me. I am not interested in turning Canada into some economic backwater. I am not interested in seeing Canada drop back from the at least reasonably acceptable levels of protection for humans and for the environment which are established. I am not interested in providing an opportunity for someone to walk in with a handful of down-payment dollars, borrow the balance from Canadian banking and financial institutions, turn all of that into a tenfold profit, then put it all in his pocket and walk away. I am not interested in that. That does not help Canada and certainly does not provide anything of value. There is no lasting value in an operation which will put $100,000 or $100 million into Canada if its only purpose is to close the plant down, take the profits it was able to make and ultimately move back to where it came from or to some other part of the world, in order to begin the exercise all over again. I feel the Government has an obligation to consider that prospect. It has an obligation to try to understand that that is the way the system works.
December 11, 1984

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has raised a very important question. However, Bill C-209 respecting the execution of mass murders only deals with part of the problem in my opinion. I think that its scope should be extended.
What I do not understand is that although our constituents have made this a priority issue the Government opposite is showing no leadership on the question of the death penalty. When I was elected in 1979, one of the first things I did was to ask my constituents this question in a householder mailing: Do you agree with a return of the death penalty? 85 per cent of them answered yes. This was the opinion of my constituents in 1979. They were for a return of the death penalty. Each week,
1 receive letters from people throughout the country. In nine out of ten cases, people favour a return of the death penalty.
In terms of human tragedy, we often forget those who are the real victims. It is not only the one who is killed whose rights are violated, but all those around him who love him, his father, his mother, his sons, his daughters, his brothers and his sisters, and the spouse who go through a very harrowing and even traumatic experience.
The major problem revolves around the application of the law. If our institutions are unable to keep convicts in jail and if the convicts continue to escape, our correctional system should be reformed. How many times do we read in the newspapers that people on parole have committed another crime? How many times do we hear that they have committed acts of violence and even murders? The Government should have the courage, first of all, to submit the issue of the death penalty to a free vote in this House, and second, to review our parole system.
Mr. Speaker, I know that other Members want to speak, but in closing, I could perhaps suggest that we consider having a national referendum on the death penalty. I often have the feeling that some Members in this House are saying that their constituents want the death penalty, but that they themselves are against it. Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) for raising this matter. The Government does not significantly differ from the position he stated, but for the record I think it would be appropriate that I review the history of this situation.
On October 12, the International Court of Justice established the Maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine. That is the boundary, it is final and not in dispute. Indeed, in this House On December 5, in response to a question from the Hon. Member, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) put the position of the Government of Canada very clearly.
Before going to the International Court of Justice, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that Canada had negotiated and signed a treaty with the Americans which would have provided for reciprocal fishing rights and joint management of certain Gulf of Maine stocks, so that both countries would have experienced minimum changes to their established fishing patterns wherever the International Court of Justice might place the Maritime boundary between them. In the end this agreement was rejected by the U.S. Senate. The Americans have now proposed that both countries continue fishing as before in the former disputed area for a period of one year while they assess the implications of the decision and develop their position for such further negotiations as might be necessary in respect of East Coast fishery resources.
An official proposal on these lines was received from the U.S. Government on December 7. It acknowledges the final and binding character of the boundary fixed by the International Court of Justice. The Ministers concerned have not yet had an opportunity to finalize a formal response. However, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated publicly that we do not envision agreeing to the proposal. We have serious doubts about it.
One of our concerns is to avoid a return, however temporary, to a situation where unrestrained fishing might again threaten the living resources of the Gulf of Maine area. Our primary objective is to get on with managing the resource in a
Adjournment Debate
manner that will maintain it and, if possible, let it return to previous levels so that we can protect the jobs of Canadians involved in the fishing industry.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans scientists are working on an analysis of the resources in the Canadian zone in close consultation with the industry. When this analysis is completed, and only then, will we be in a position to determine precisely what we need to do to manage our resources and what we need in the way of co-operation from the Americans.

The writ empowers the officers named to search any place, including a dwelling or a house, at any time in the execution of their duties, to enforce the relevant Act. The writ empowers its holders to enter any place without requesting entry, to break open doors, chests, locks and containers. It is valid as long as the holders are officers under the Acts. I have already described telewarrants. The United States has been using telewarrants for 14 years. They have consistently withstood constitutional challenges. Telewarrants must be taken under oath and recorded by the justice who issues them. Research has been done in this area, mostly by civil liberties groups, and it has been found that there is broad support for this procedure in the legal community.

It would seem to be unnecessarily harmful to the persons whose premises had been searched to have their names reported and publicized in the event that a charge is not laid. It could affect their reputations. The amendment would impose restrictions on publishing the facts of the search, unless the persons involved gave their consent or charges were laid.
Another area in the legislation deals with solicitor/client privilege. If documents are seized from the possession of lawyers and they claim that the documents are privileged, the documents can still be seized but they would be placed in a sealed packet and would only be made available to the prosecution if a judge made the finding that the documents were not protected by the solicitor/client privilege.
There is a provision in the Bill which calls for the prompt return of seized property. We have all happened upon people who were quite annoyed because they had suffered a theft or a break-in and their property had to be used as evidence in court proceedings. It often takes months, sometimes years, before that property is returned to those individuals. The proposed amendments will require reviews to be made at each stage of the proceedings, and will require that such property be quickly returned to the owners.

The objective is to provide reasonably priced housing, of which there is a shortage in the north as there is in many other places throughout Canada. The request for this legislation comes from the Government of the Northwest Territories and individual MLAs from all three political Parties represented. It also comes from the City of Yellowknife, in particular, and His Worship the Mayor, Don Sian, and from the real estate fraternity as well as from individuals who would like the opportunity to own and invest in condominiums.
When condominiums started to be constructed throughout Canada, in 1969 a condominium ordinance was passed by the Territorial Legislature. It is, Sir, a model Act. It is based on provincial Acts. It does not diverge from them in any way. I suspect the advice of the law commissioners was taken in the drafting of this legislation. It governs the regulation of condominium corporations, the title to common areas by condominium corporations, title to individual units therein, and the relationships between a condominium corporation and the holders of individual units. However, it was found that there was a conflict with the federal Act, the Land Titles Act. As a consequence, the condominium ordinance was ultra vires.
What we are trying to do today is to put this matter to right. The Land Titles Act has a long and honourable history going back to Confederation. It deals with things like the concepts of dower and courtesy. Anybody who is familiar with medieval matrimonial law will know all about this, but it does not deal with the condominium concept. was not around at the time of Confederation. Since that time, the Province of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have all enacted their own land titles legislation.
In January, 1981, Bill C-52 was introduced into the House of Commons. This would have put the situation right. It would have done two things. Mr. Speaker, I see that the Conservatives are touchy. BasePK: 3508606

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, over the past few weeks I have received scores of telephone calls from Armed Forces personnel who are concerned about the effect that the UI changes to earnings will have on them when they retire. Members of the Armed Forces are required to retire by the age of 55, or after 25 years of service.
One of the recognized and very much deserved benefits of serving with the Armed Forces is the accumulation of severance benefits. The Conservative Government has announced that, as of March 31, 1985, those payments will be considered as income for unemployment insurance purposes. I understand from the Minister's office that the rollover provisions that allow severance benefits to be placed into an RRSP, so that they will not be considered as income for income tax purposes, will not apply for UI purposes. This essentially wipes out the value of those severance payments that were formerly considered a working benefit.
Many of those who retire from the Armed Forces continue to work until the usual retirement age of 65, and continue to make UI contributions during those working years. The Government has announced that pension income will be considered income for UI purposes, essentially making those retirees ineligible for UI benefits. Due to the early retirement age of Armed Forces personnel, they have been placed in the very unique situation of being required to pay into an insurance program, the Unemployment Insurance Program, without being eligible to collect benefits from that program. I suggest to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that these discriminatory aspects of UI changes should be reconsidered.

The same Bill has been proposed many times before by Members of the New Democratic Party. I heard Mr. Yurko, the former Member for Edmonton East, make the same proposal. There have been many statements under S.O. 43. However, I must admit I have rarely heard any statements or views on the subject by Members from Quebec. I speak today as an Ontarian by birth, with a solid Irish, Scotch and French background, and I would ask those Members in this House who are from Quebec to take part in the debate so that we will finally know where they stand and what their position is on an issue that has been a very important one in this country. The House will remember that Ontario was the bad guy and that Quebec was "deeply offended" by what happened, which gave rise to some serious problems with respect to Canadian unity.
I think this will be an opportunity for our Quebec Members ... I see the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) who often speaks during the hour for private Members, and I wonder whether she would be willing to state her views on this important matter. I am sure she is well up on the subject and would be able to give us some clarification regarding the views of those Quebec Members who all too often remain silent on such important issues.
Louis David Riel

Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) a very important question regarding his Government's approach to the young people of this country and the availability, access and opportunity for them to have a college or university education, a post-secondary education. 1 asked this question because of the cuts made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his economic statement in the fall, and because of my grave concern for the future of the young people of this country. Adjournment Debate
cent of high school drop-outs were not able to obtain employment.
Professor David Foot, professor of economics at the University of Toronto, who is an expert renowned in his field, has made extensive labour-market studies and has given us ample evidence that education is fundamental to providing a worthwhile future, a future with decent and relevant employment for our young people, and is also vital to the future of our great country and its economy.

The students of Canada and the people of Canada are entitled to a clear

Mr. Speaker, on November 14 I asked the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism (Mr. Murta) a couple of questions dealing with the report of the Special Parliamentary Committee on Visible Minorities, and I followed with a query about the awaited report from Judge Abella. Admittedly and understandably the answers I received were quite tentative. I requested then the opportunity to speak further on the matter. Now, about two and a half months later and more than twice as far into the life of the present Government as we were at that time, it is appropriate to consider the record of the Government to this point. Also it is appropriate to inquire about the possibilities of early action and to press for that early action which various members of the Canadian community, visible minorities of all sorts, have been hoping for so long.
The report Equality Now focused on the need for action in a great variety of areas, but I want to focus particularly on the employment recommendations. Of course, the Abella report contained concerns about equity in employment. That was its main focus.
The record of the Government to this point has not been very reassuring. The recommendation to establish a Department of Multiculturalism never had the support of the Conservative Party. Presumably it will not be a policy of the Government now. That is to be greatly regretted because it is important to have someone responsible, a minister with a department and substantial resources, in order to achieve the ends for which so many Canadians hoped. Whether we will have a standing committee perhaps is not entirely in the hands of the Government. It is likely that recommendations 25 and 26 of the report will not be acted upon. One is tempted to conclude that we are likely to see the same contrast between rhetoric and reality which characterized preceding Liberal Governments ever since the policy of multiculturalism was enunciated in 1971.
Another area of concern is that of appointments to various boards, commissions and other offices which the federal government control. An assessment of the actions of the new Government, whatever the protestations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have been, again have been disappointing. There were precious few appointments of people from the visible minorities, from the ethno-cultural diversity of the country. However, I am pleased to see that Francophones and women fared rather better in appointments.
Recommendation 21 of the Commission still awaits action. The activities of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism vis-a-vis the National Association of Japanese Canadians in the last few weeks, focusing on recommendation 33 of the report, again arouse concern. There is no readiness to negotiate a very narrow concern about redress for that aggrieved
community. I only hope that my expression of concern proves to be unjustified.
These particular decisions by the Government in past weeks leave one concerned about the extent to which there will be action in areas of employment. Surely employment is ultimately the area in which there has to be action if the report Equality Now and the Abella report are to mean anything at all to Canadian society in general.
The various recommendations in Equality Now call for the early establishment of a five-year program by the federal Government with regard to the various corporations and institutions that it was involved with, a well formulated five-year program designed to achieve a measure of voluntary compliance and tests of it. As far as corporations doing business with the Government were concerned, the report called for contract compliance provisions to be established.
These recommendations in the Equality Now report were reflected in the Abella report in various ways, focusing on means by which equity in employment might be achieved. The judge has done a magnificent job in clarifying means in law and in institutions, in new provisions designed to smooth the way for a broader participation in employment among Canadians. These recommendations have had the support of various important bodies. The Canadian Ethno-Cultural Council and the Canadian Human Rights Commission have both recommended actions along these lines. I await the response of the Parliamentary Secretary.

Mr. Speaker, when we broke for lunch I was discussing the possibility of amalgamating the existing insurance plan in western Canada with the Western Grain Stabilization Plan in order to have an over-all plan which would be much more effective and valuable. The existing insurance plan provides a structure which covers most of the Prairies. The provincial Governments provide the administration, the federal Government provides a portion of the funds and the farmers also make a contribution to the plan. If that approach were tailored to the needs of every farmer, they would be better off in the end. It would allow the stabilization plan to be tailored for each farmer, region and crop. If the Government intends to amend the Act later in the year to look at this type of approach, we would be happy to exchange a more comprehensive plan for the present Western Grain Stabilization Plan.
I do not think the Government has made a commitment, nor do I think it is prepared to make the kind of commitment, which would provide income security to grain farmers. There are a number of areas in the Act which need to be reviewed.
When the Act was passed in 1978, a number of Members in the House suggested that certain amendments should be made. Since that time the Act has been amended several times and members of the NDP have reiterated the fact that there are weaknesses in the Act which should be corrected. We would congratulate the Minister if it is his intention to amend the Act. We hope that it is done very quickly. After this amendment is passed and the pay-out is made, the Act could be brought before the House to remedy some of its shortcomings.
Over the years members of the New Democratic Party have suggested four or Five policy changes with respect to the Act. If we are unable to get an agricultural income security program or a grain producers' income insurance plan, we will not be able to look at it on a total basis as far as the Prairies are concerned. The Act should be changed so that it will be more effective in the future.
I know many government Members share our concerns, because when the House was debating the Act last year they

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act mentioned approaches which are similar to those which I will suggest today.
First, we believe that the plan should be more producer-specific. There should be a factor which allows a better definition of individual problems. For example, many of the farmers who are going under today are good farmers, but because they are beginning their farms, because of their debt load and because of high interest rates they are unable to meet their payments and continue having a good cash flow. A guaranteed cash flow would be worthwhile to them. However, we are not able to target money for that group. In our wisdom, if we looked at it we might decide that that is not an area where our concern should be targeted.
Second, we believe that the pay-out should be on a regional basis. I think there are very good examples for this which the Government has made some movement toward alleviating. For example, with respect to the western drought, and specifically the drought in southern Saskatchewan, if the rest of the provinces had a good crop and the prices were fairly high, southern Saskatchewan would not be able to get any money from the fund. Therefore we believe that we should be able to make those payments on a regional basis.
Another example would be the frost which on occasion has devastated crops in the Peace River area. Northeast Saskatchewan has had a considerable amount of flood damage in the past few years. Again, that area could have been targeted as a region which should have received money. If the majority of regions in the Praries have a good crop, there is no reason that a region which is hit by poor weather and therefore has a poor crop should not be able to get funds from the plan. That is why the plan is there.
Third, we believe that the plan should be more grain-specific. It should be grain specific because more and more of the farm population are specializing. Most of their crop will be peas, lentils or canola, barley or flax. Most have established some kind of rotation which is better for the land, but we still have those people who specialize in one or two grains. What happens if one crop fails? Maybe only one farmer in ten is affected by that failure, but if all of his land is in canola and there is no crop or the bottom drops out of the market, he is affected. Should he not have more of a call on stabilization in those kinds of circumstances? We think we should look at that.
The plan should be more oriented to the cost of production. That has been talked about on all sides of the House and there is a provision in the present formula, but we still have to recognize that at present the pay-out of stabilization payments is related more to cash income than the cost of production.
There is no real provision for labour, management or cost of investment, or even poor delivery opportunities. Perhaps that is one of the major factors. Right now we do not have too much trouble getting our grain to market because we have so little of it out in the west due to the drought. But there have been many years where we had poor delivery possibilities. In some cases we had two years of grain in the bin. Those kinds of
situations occur so the plan should be related more to farm income.
The Wheat Pool has made a suggestion which I think is worth looking at. They have suggested that farmers who grow their own feed grains should have an opportunity to pay the levy on that grain so that if they have a poor crop they will qualify for stabilization payments. It might be a little difficult to establish but it would be fair and worthwhile for those farmers who raise their own cattle and hog feed.

They are concerned, just to make the case which I understand they make, that if we remove capital gains tax we allow people to come in who want to speculate on land and hold it against inflation. This is exactly what I hope will happen in committee. We will certainly be looking at those three issues in committee.
In conclusion, if we look at some of the things the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) has been doing in terms of the way Section 31 has been administered, I think he is making some strides in having his Department better understand exactly what makes a farmer or what constitutes a genuine farmer and what does not. In my constituency, I know of cases that have been sorted out since the Minister of National Revenue has been there. That has gone a long way, or at least a partial way, in addressing some of the concerns that we have over Section 31.

Adjournment Debate
national debt. For example, the ongoing operating costs associated with the institute in Manitoba would have been in excess of $20 million per year.

The Minister has already received several substantive proposals on the use of the facility. Nevertheless, the federal Government welcomes further input and representations by interested Hon. Members of this House.

Mr. Speaker, today Canada and other Commonwealth countries encircling the globe are observing Commonwealth Day. It was a Canadian proposal made ten years ago at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Jamaica that one day should be set aside each year to mark our membership in this singular organization. The second Monday in March was chosen not to be a holiday but to be an occasion when most children would be in school and could participate in special projects to increase their understanding of the Commonwealth. Its continued vitality depends upon the interest and involvement of all of our citizens, but particularly of younger Canadians.

The United Nations has declared this year the International Year of Youth. The Commonwealth countries are planning to organize a number of special events, the main one being a gathering of young people from all Commonwealth countries who will be coming to Ottawa in June to discuss the challenges of the 80s.
The number of Commonwealth bursaries offered by Canada has been raised from 300 to 500. Since the program was established in 1959, when it was first suggested by the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the time, Mr. Sidney Smith, more than 20,000 Commonwealth students have been able to benefit from these bursaries.
Canada remains convinced that this program and other training programs are useful because our country sees the youth of the Commonwealth countries as a guarantee that the Commonwealth will remain in the same excellent condition it is now.

We live in an age, Sir, of hardening ideologies, of increasing economic disparities and growing cultural nationalism, yet the Commonwealth association cuts across all of these barriers. Its 49 members represent every geographical, political, economic and social group in the world. Nevertheless, it has many things in common; a shared working language, the heritage of common law and parliamentary traditions and, most importantly, the tradition of a frank and pragmatic approach to problem solving. The latter part of this century has been called the "era of negotiation" but it is witnessing a crisis in the world's multilateral system. We believe that the Commonwealth, with its special qualities, can be an example to other international bodies.
With this in mind, it is fitting, Mr. Speaker, that we commemorate this unique family of nations and reaffirm Canada's commitment to the future of the Commonwealth.

ic development of this region and the province of Quebec as a whole.

On that date, I asked whether the government was looking into the possibility of becoming a shareholder in the Domtar Corporation, and whether this was one of the alternatives being considered. Moreover, I was seeking the assurance that it would not discriminate against that company on the ground that 45 p. 100 of the shares were held by agencies of the Quebec government. Indeed, we learned during the weekend that Domtar was now considering a major investment in Minnesota, which would mean a lot for the fine paper market in the United States and effectively prevent this project from going forward in the Eastern Townships, even though it would benefit the economy of Quebec and create jobs for Quebecers in that region.
However, what disturbs us is the contradiction between the official statements made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Last November 8, Mr. Speaker, the Department announced the changes to be made to the Industrial and Regional Development Program. Among the changes introduced last November 8, apparently as part of the new governmental policy, the Department stated that, in the future, Crown corporations would not be entitled to any subsidies. This policy was confirmed in the estimates of the Minister which were published only two weeks ago. This is indeed departmental policy and it is quite clear that departmental officials understand this to mean that Crown corporations and their subsidiaries, such as Domtar, will no longer be able to receive subsidies or financial assistance from the Government. However, when we asked the Prime Minister about it, he said: "No, that is not my policy." In fact, on March 1, he said that this was the interpretation of the departmental officials not his own nor that of his colleagues. These interpretations are completely contradictory, Mr. Speaker.
Adjournment Debate
Even more recently, on March 11, the Minister finally came back to the House, and in reply to the questions addressed to him, he said that these two statements, namely that of the Prime Minister to the effect that Domtar could receive subsidies, and the statement of his department that a company such as Domtar would not be eligible or entitled to subsidies, were quite consistent with each other, in spite of the obvious contradiction.
Second, Mr. Speaker, what disturbs me as the spokesman for my Party, is not simply the discrimination directed against a Crown corporation or its subsidiary, but also the discrimination against poor provinces and especially the Province of Quebec.
In Quebec, the industrial structure is quite different from the one in Ontario, for instance, because of the Caisse de depot et de placement du Quebec, because of the intervention of the Societe generate de financement, and because the public sector is involved in provincial industries in a way unparalleled in other provinces. This fact was ignored in the policy announced by the Minister on November 8.
Mr. Speaker, this is why we are not satisfied with the replies of the Government.

Great Britain seems to be having less and less use for its House of Peers. However, Great Britain is stuck with its House of Peers because its peers are hereditary. I do not see any reason to continue the pretence that we in Canada have a reformed version of the House of Peers.
I think that having two Houses simply confuses the public and divides the jurisdictions. We now have constitutional problems between Ottawa and the provinces but to emphasize further a division between the Senate and the House of Commons only makes legislation more difficult to understand by the people on the street and in fact more difficult to understand by those who are making the legislation.
The argument that we need all wear two hats, one Canadian and one regional, is an old argument. In fact, I suppose it was the argument used, in those words or others, when the Senate was first created in the last century. It is a very abstract argument, and interestingly enough it is used principally by those who wish to maintain the status quo, by those who want to keep change limited and by those who do not want any real transfer of power from the wealthy to the less wealthy.
The Senate has been a very good bulwark of the wealthy. Whenever a Parliament, under pressure from the public, puts through legislation to limit the powers of the banks, by the time the Bill gets through the Senate the Senate has enlarged the powers of the banks. The Senate has many ties with the banks. Not all Senators do; there are a few who do not have ties with the banks. However, the job Senators do on banking legislation is certainly very valuable to the banks and very harmful to the farmers, working people and small-businessmen who must suffer the results of lopsided legislation in favour of the banks.
The argument that national unity is protected by a second House has nothing to recommend it. It has never been demonstrated that it would in fact promote national unity. What it does is perpetuate a system in which issues of real importance to working people and farmers are befuddled either by appeals to solve this mysterious problem between the French and the English or between the English and people of other languages or the mysterious problem of the regions. Problems do not get solved by having a Senate; they simply become more mystifying.
This motion calls upon us to examine the Senate Reform report, and I would support the motion for that purpose. However, when we do examine the report, I do not really think we will find its recommendations workable. I think it is necessary to go through those recommendations, find that they are not workable, and then deal with what has for half a century been the only clearly workable solution to the Senate problem, and that is abolition.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak again to Bill C-24 on oil substitution and conservation and on home insulation. One of the real values of keeping this Bill before the House as long as it has been is that it gives the opportunity to people to let us know exactly how they feel about this Bill. Since I last spoke on the Bill a couple of weeks ago I have had about 20 letters, almost all taking the same position. People need this oil substitution Bill extended rather than cut. The idea of keeping a Bill before the House and maybe hoisting it for six months allows the public to take a good look at the Bill, to judge it and then let us know how they feel about it.
I strongly support a motion to hoist this Bill because that will give not only the people of Canada an opportunity to take a look at this Bill, but it will also give an opportunity to the present Government to back off and make use of the Bill in a different way.
As a matter of interest, I want to list a number of reasons that have been conveyed to me in letters from my constituents. The reason that comes most often from my constituency is that gas supply is just now reaching a person's farm or house. If this Bill cuts off the opportunity for substitution, that person will not be able to take advantage of the structure presently in place. Is that fair, Mr. Speaker? Just because gas does not reach an individual's home until this summer or the summer after, is he not going to be able to take advantage of the substitution grants?
A second reason and one which has been mentioned many times already is that the ground is frozen. People will not be able to dig until after April. Therefore a person is forced into a position where he will get less of the substitution grant than someone who was able to take advantage of it last fall.
The third reason one hears is from the person who has been planning to substitute his energy supply for years. Now he is only going to be able to do about half as much work as before. Another reason is that a person would have been able to afford conversion but cannot now because the grant will not be as big as expected. All of this is information that has been passed to us from our constituents.
I have not received-and I think the same goes for my colleagues-as many letters from people worried about the loss of CHIP grants, probably because that program has been used much more extensively and has not been dependent upon the availability of gas or other forms of fuel. However, the general tenor of the letters has been much the same, that it is unfair to take away these grants since some people have not had an opportunity to make use of them while other people, even in the same areas, have had an opportunity to do so. The other
March 18, 1985

main point of view has been that future increases in costs of fuels will make them take advantage of the grant and therefore they would like that opportunity. Some people have indicated that they could not afford to do it before but will have to do it in the future, so why should they not receive the same support as have other people in the past?
There are a number of points which should be put on the record before we let the Bill go to committee or hopefully hoist it for six months, so that the Government can take a look at the effect of the Bill. This has been one of the most popular grant programs across the country. In fact, it might be the best possible job-creation program around. When a few dollars are put into the hands of people to make their homes more energy efficient, they usually make other improvements as well. Perhaps it would be best to expand this program and put more money into the hands of home owners so that they can improve the quality of their homes. These grants, along with RRAP grants, have almost been direct job-creation programs because as soon as the money is available to home owners to improve their homes, they hire someone to do the work. It is also a direct job-creation program in that it has a direct effect upon small businesses in the communities where the money is spent. Home owners purchase new furnaces and have them installed; home owners purchase insulation and have it installed. Its cancellation is unfair and discriminatory because a large group of the population has not had an opportunity to substitute oil with some different fuel. They are quite willing to do so now that a substitute fuel is becoming available to them.
Many speakers on the Government side have suggested that these grants went to higher income groups. A study conducted by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources indicates something quite different. Since these grants were taxable, the taxation system took away a certain portion of the amount payable, particularly for higher income groups. The Government is suggesting by this cut that it is no longer interested in conservation or in assisting lower income Canadians to reduce their costs. It has said that it will let the oil go to the world price and that it will not put in place a mechanism for people who cannot afford the world price to improve their homes so that they will not use as much oil. The money saved in conservation by individual home owners, as far as the Government is concerned, is money that it will not have to put out to purchase foreign oil.
Consequently, the business direction in this Bill is not for the good of the people, for the good of the country or for the good of the Government. Therefore it should take advantage of our hoist motion and keep this Bill off the books for at least six months, until it analyses its effects.

Any programs that were designed to cut housing costs would be supported by almost anyone in the country, except this Conservative Government. This is a country in which we have limited oil resources. It is a non-renewable resource. Any program designed to conserve oil would make sense to anyone in this country, with the possible exception of this Conservative Government.
Imported oil is costly. It is needed in the east particularly. Any program designed to reduce imports of oil from elsewhere would, I am sure, be supported by almost everyone in this country, again with the exception of this Conservative Government. Unemployment is a critical program and any program designed to produce jobs would be approved by anybody in this country, except the Conservative Government. Indeed, because COSP and CHIP contribute to all these goals, they would be supported by almost everyone in the country. We must ask ourselves: Why are they not supported by the Conservative Government?
The Canadian Oil Substitution Program was introduced in 1980 to reduce oil use from 37 per cent to 10 per cent of residential energy. It means that the consumer will receive a return on his investment within two to three years.

Many of the people who converted were low-income citizens. Indeed, a great proportion of the grants went to those who earned less than $15,000 a year. Those who took advantage of the cuts in fuel costs were able to reduce their expenses by 17 per cent through CHIP. It amounted to a saving of $207 per year. Therefore, they paid for their conversion within one year. Through CHIP, 23,000 barrels of oil per day were saved. A person who took advantage of both COSP and CHIP saved approximately $800 a year.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the request of my hon. friend with respect to the desire of the Government to make a statement about the situation of the Canadian Commercial Bank. Notice of the desire of the Government to make a statement about this matter at eleven o'clock this morning reached me only about 40 minutes ago. We have been reflecting on that request. Bearing in mind the sensitivity of the situation and what the Government House Leader said about the importance of being able to put questions on the matter in a parliamentary way, it is our preference that the statement be made at the usual time at three o'clock. This would give our spokespersons a chance to review the statement in advance-we have not seen it-and to reflect upon our questions.
I point out to the House that early this morning a rather detailed press release on this was issued by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). That press release has also been the subject of news reports as early as nine o'clock this morning. I am not complaining about that; I am just saying that it is not necessary to have a statement in the House at eleven o'clock to inform either the public or the House of the situation. Therefore, under the circumstances outlined by my hon. friend with respect to the sensitivity of this situation, I think it would be most helpful to the House, in terms of the kind of response we could give to the Government statement and the kinds of questions we could ask, if we had time to reflect upon the matter until the usual time for making statements on motions at three o'clock this afternoon.

Good. Let me say to the Hon. Member who asked the question that there is nothing wrong with consultation, but consultation is not a substitute for action. When the Government of today was elected in 1984, its members had left the impression with the public of Canada that not only had they identified the problems, but that they had solutions. They asked for support on the basis of being able to put forward a new agenda for Canada, an agenda which would include solutions to the problems which they had identified when they were in opposition.

The Government's obligation is to bring forward its proposals so that they can be debated by those people who attended the conference and by the House of Commons. Then it should proceed with whatever consensus develops as a result of the debate. If it goes out and seeks consensus for the next four years, we will be in the same position as the one in which we are today, come the next election.

BasePK: 3520071

Speech:
I would like to address the question of employment in 1985. The Hon. Member, as an astute observer of the economic process, will understand the nature of business cycles. When times are good, there is high employment creation. But the normal forces of the economy will cause that business cycle to turn down at any given period of time. We are now in the late stages of a business cycle, so there is a natural process of downturn. We are attempting to adjust upward that downturn through the policies which we have introduced.
As I indicated on November 8, we were looking at some slowdown during the course of the business cycle. I made it quite clear at that time that there would probably be some slowdown in the economic process in 1985. However, since November, people-not me, but business people and economists-have said that they have higher expectations of growth in the economy because of the things that the Government is doing. Therefore, we are looking for better economic growth in 1985 than was expected at the end of 1984. That is progress. It is not as much progress as I would like but we are moving in the right direction.
The Hon. Member said that by my statement on Friday morning at the National Economic Conference I was foreclosing on the consultative process. I am not doing so. If he had read my speech he would not have made that comment. Yes, I did say we are committed to a reduction in the deficit. I am surprised that that Hon. Member, of all Hon. Members in the Opposition Parties, should be attacking me for trying to get a greater degree of control over the deficit, because he himself has stated on many occasions that the deficit, at $35 billion, is far too high. What we are saying is we are open to consultation on how much and how fast, and I received good ideas on that. I think that was a very helpful part of the process last weekend.
Let me also ask the Hon. Member to broaden his horizons a little, to not just look at the deficit but at the range of issues I discussed in my speech. Other areas were discussed, such as trade, technology, training, and all of these things about which I set the stage in my opening remarks to encourage discussion by participants at the conference so that we could benefit from the views of the Canadians who were represented there.
The Hon. Member asked why we did not set out position papers for the Economic Conference. I ask him to think back-although it is a long time ago-to November 8. We did set out in the economic statement in November a very clear statement of the range of options which were open to us. It was a very extensive position paper, if you will, which covered a number of items which we felt should be discussed. That was the framework of reference for most of the topics which were discussed in the Economic Conference.
Let me outline some of those topics. Research and development; technology; training; investment, particularly for small business; trade; policy and trade promotion; unemployment insurance reform; and how to deal with the problems of access to capital by small business, women and minority groups. These were all signalled in the statement of November 8.
That was the framework for discussion at the Economic Conference this past weekend. It was also the framework for discussion in the consultative process which was carried out by many of my colleagues in the Government and it has been responded to in a very healthy and positive way by Canadians right across the country.

Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking earlier, I had begun to talk about trade arrangements between Canada and the United States. I had been pointing out that while our relationship with out greatest ally and chief trading partner is extremely important to us, it is also important that we negotiate well in all these matters because the United States has certainly shown itself very adroit in protecting its own interests in the past.
The United States complained long and hard about our Foreign Investment Review Agency, but that country itself prohibits or restricts foreign investment in many sectors of its economy-in coastal and freshwater shipping, aviation, nuclear and hydro generating, communications, financial industries, real estate, fishing, some mineral leases, dredging and salvaging operations, and the defence industries. As the House knows, the net of defence industries is cast very wide.
A comparison of relative investment is quite interesting. For instance, mining is approximately 40 per cent foreign controlled in Canada and approximately 5 per cent in the United States; oil and gas, something between 50 per cent and 60 per cent foreign controlled in Canada as against 18 per cent in the U.S.; and manufacturing, something around 48 per cent foreign controlled in Canada compared with 3 per cent in the United States. The whole basis on which to consider investment policy in the two countries is different.
The U.S. economy, which is so greatly admired by the Government opposite, is not without problems. Some of those problems may impact upon us unless we plan carefully to protect ourselves. The United States has an enormous trade deficit. If at some point it becomes concerned about it and decides to act on it, we will certainly be open to injury. For instance, Ontario alone exports more into the United States than does Japan. The United States also has an enormous deficit which, of course, is fuelled by enormous defence spending. This is a situation which may change. International banking institutions may very well become concerned about the fact that the United States is so greatly over-extended by some standards. If there are major changes in the way the international community looks at this, we might be very vulnerable if indeed we have put all our eggs into that basket without proper negotiation and safeguards.
Approximately 80 per cent of our trade is now with the United States. Does the Government plan to leave that more or less as it is and to continue, as did the Liberal Government, to encourage exporters to find other markets, particularly Pacific Rim countries, or is the intention to lock us in more closely with the United States? These are things to which we should know the answers.
In talking about trade arrangements, particularly a trade treaty with the United States, it is impossible to do that unless one also looks at the whole question of emerging technologies, emerging competition from the less developed countries, the effect of this on our own industries and the need to protect our people, be it with retraining grants or labour adjustment programs. This whole package needs to be considered very carefully.
It may very well be that the Government is considering all this, but we do not know because less and less is being debated in this House. All of us were elected by people who have had
March 25, 1985

an enormously difficult time living through the recession. They are hurting and are looking for some help.

Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that the last Member who spoke has to smile. He remembers that it was his Liberal Government which cut the entire amount of money from those provinces.
We welcome the Government's move, although we do recognize that it does not provide for the entire shortfall that the poorer provinces in this country are facing as a result of the equalization provision that was passed by the Liberal Government in 1982.
It is important that we all remember that when this Government came into power, it was not its intention to move on equalization payments. The briefing notes which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) left in Winnipeg indicated that he was prepared to give a negative repsonse to the people of that province. Later in this House, in answer to questions by myself, he tried to state that the federal Government's financial position was worse vis-a-vis that of the recipient provinces. I believe that is a position which is completely indefensible.
Throughout the period of this Conservative Government, it has pretended that it was some kind of surprise to find that there was an actual decline in the money that would be going to the provinces as a result of the 1982 legislation. Yet in 1982 Conservative Opposition Members stood with Members of the New Democratic Party like the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and fought against the equalization formula the Liberal Government had then introduced. Some of those Members are now members of the Cabinet and they must act upon the words they spoke in 1982. I for one am glad that the Government has made a partial reinstatement of the money to those provinces.
Although this announcement will benefit a number of provinces, it is obvious to all that it was the New Democratic Party Government of Manitoba that led and forced the fight on this issue. The Manitoba Government, along with a coalition of representatives from labour, health, education and social services groups, confronted the federal Government. To a degree, they were successful. It is their victory and we in the House

should give them that credit. When the legislation comes before the House, we will deal with it further.
At this time I would like to say that there are still concerns with which we must deal. We need more information about what the provinces will actually receive in 1986-87. We also need to know the effect of federal cut-backs, including those that will be in the upcoming Budget, and how that will affect the economic situation of the provinces. We must also have information on when there will actually be tax reform in t his nation so that those who can afford to pay will pay their fair share.
In closing, I must point out that we need to know the position of the Government with regard to negotiations that will be taking place for the 1987-92 agreement. Concerning this last point, it is essential that the federal Government not look only at its deficit position but also to providing those poor provinces with the ability to provide services to their citizens. That was the purpose of equalization payments and that is why it is in the Constitution.
This is a victory for the people of Manitoba, Quebec and the other provinces that will be receiving more funding as a result of this legislation about which we learned today, but we must also tell Canadians that they are entitled to a certain basic level of services regardless of where they live. Canadian sugar-beet producers. In Ottawa today we have over 100 representatives of the 1,500 Canadian sugar-beet producers, from Alberta, Manitoba, and Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate, following up on a question I asked on April 2 of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). The question dealt with the recent report of Conservative Members on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which suggested that our immigration levels be increased in the coming years largely with immigrants who are entrepreneurs. In very simple, everyday language the recommendation suggested that immigration increases should only involve rich immigrants.
My question on April 2 was whether the Minister agreed with this premise and whether she was prepared to act on it, or whether she was prepared to replace that with a thorough and genuine parliamentary process in close concert with Canadians. At the time the Minister was not in the House. The Acting Minister got up, ranted and raved, but went around the issue quite nicely. I am hopeful that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister will provide some sense of leadership and given an answer to the question.
Adjournment Debate
My Party and I are certainly not opposed to having entrepreneurs consider Canada their new home. We encourage and support that. In fact, the entrepreneur stream within the immigration policy was instituted by this Party while it was in Government. However, we feel that rich immigrants should not be the cornerstone of an immigration policy. To embark on this path would be to turn back the clock on what has been the development of a progressive and compassionate policy within the context of a multicultural and multilingual Canada. That policy values the principle of family re-unification and the principle of assisting family streams so that Canadians can have the opportunity of sponsoring relatives and friends from abroad.
I would like to quote the recommendation which is really the essence of the report. It is Item 9 under Economic Considerations. It reads:
When the economic consideration is paramount in increasing the immigration level, then the fundamental principle should be the active recruitment of people who are either self-supporting, or who can clearly contribute to the growth of the Canadian economy. For example: those who fit current regulations for entrepreneurial immigration ... bring with them investment capital which they will use to create new jobs and export potential,... self-employed immigrants, etc. The current consultation process for 1986 should focus on ways to encourage, in every possible way, increasing the number of people whose immigration to Canada would enhance our economic capacity.
A recent article in The Toronto Star quoted the chairman of that Standing Committee who suggested that the ideal immigrant:
-should come from a developed nation, preferably the U.S. or one of the Western European countries-should have a good business background, equity capital in the neighbourhood of $500,000 and an impulse to create.
I am surprised that the chairman did not go further and propose that specifications on an individual's hair colour, weight and height be added to the list of criteria that he has outlined for this Parliament.
The essence of the matter is that the guts of this report completely overlooks the contributions that thousands upon thousands of poor and average income immigrants have made to this country, and that the Government is trying to suggest that if you do not happen to be rich then you have not or cannot contribute to the economic growth of this country. That premise is completely false. The premise is that thousands of immigrants, poor and average income immigrants, have contributed to this country and have taken jobs. They have become successful businessmen, and that will continue to be the case in future.
The direction is very worrisome but the process by which the directions were formulated are equally as worrisome, Mr. Speaker. There was not one single witness outside of employment and immigration employees to appear before the committee. There was not one ethno-cultural group invited, nor one immigrant aid society, nor one union, nor one professor, nor one economist. Nor was any economic study done on this question.

Mr. Speaker, I join this debate for two reasons. The first is a strong sense of concern which has come to me this past winter. Farmer after farmer in my constituency has come to speak about the extreme pressures, the crisis of credit, and the difficulty of making ends meet in one of the most productive agricultural constituencies in Canada. I speak too because I think, certainly in my constituency and in other parts of Canada as well, there is a sense of grass roots excitement and grass roots commitment to change, an approach to try to somehow give farming back the fair share which it deserves in our economy. It is a dynamism which has taken dramatic form in my constituency with the formation of a powerful and exciting group called Concerned Farmers of Essex County. It has brought hundreds of people together for a series of meetings to explore this concept of parity and to draw into a commitment to that concept not just those who are part of the organization itself, but those who are part of the broader Essex County Federation of Agriculture.
There is a sense that farmers in my constituency feel that we are finally asking the right questions when we ask how we can put a system of parity into place. They do not believe there is a simple answer to that question. They know that before succeeding in getting a price that covers their cost of production with a fair rate of return they will face serious problems because of the nature of the international economy and the difficulties of backlogs of credit with which many farmers now live. However, they have a sense that with this kind of concept and a commitment to the concept, it is possible that farmers may finally begin to get some optimism about the future. It is possible that the sons and daughters of our present farm families will finally have a sense of optimism with which they can look forward to the future.
There is a sense that in focusing on price, we are finally getting to the heart of the matter. In talking about the prices that commodities can earn, we are finally getting to the key side of the equation that affects farm households. It is important to deal with credit and the cost of credit. It is important to look at agri-bonds and tax issues, as has been done recently by the Committee on Finance, but it is even more crucial to focus on price.
April 25, 1985

The farmers in my constituency do not want something for nothing. They want the chance to earn a fair return for their work. That is why the system of parity pricing is something that they find exciting. It gives them a sense of optimism about the future.
The Bill in front of us introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), sets forth the concept. It does it in the context of western Canadian agriculture, quite frankly. People in my constituency have said that there are commodities which need to be dealt with, such as soybeans and corn which are covered by this Bill. That is a case for getting this Bill to committee and getting the committee to travel across the country to hear representations from farmers in eastern Canada as well as in western Canada. We can give those farmers a chance to grapple with this question themselves, the question of how to get the fair pricing or parity pricing that will give those farmers a future.
I support the concerned farmers of Essex County as strongly as I possibly can and I will continue to do so. I stress the point I made to them in a speech I gave a few weeks ago, and that is that this is not a partisan issue, it is an issue of justice for our farming community. This Bill will take us one step further in the right direction and I hope we can take that step here today.
