When the Government undertakes an advertising program on behalf of Tourism Canada, for example, it is contracting for so many minutes of television time, so many pages of magazine space, and so on. The commission goes to the advertising agency. There is no opportunity for cost competition. It is a professional service like any other, be it lawyers, physicians, or accountants. You are looking for quality.
I said in the House as early as last January that we are in the process of introducing a new process under which quality assessment for big contracts or departments that have large advertising budgets will be made by a panel of civil servants. With regard to the Lawson Murray contract specifically, that was a small contract. The commission to Lawson Murray was only $26,000, I think. You cannot really have a competition in a situation like that because the cost of pitching, if you brought in three, four, or five bidders, would exceed the total profit available. It would be a terrible waste of funds. You allocate that based on trust, knowledge of the individuals, and their experience.
This firm was experienced in handling financial institutions. They undertook to carry on this program which had been underway for years. They picked it up, carried it on, and said that they could reach 100 per cent of the market that we were trying to reach with these information ads with far less advertising. They showed us a new procedure for doing it. Because that advice was new to the Government, we were able to accept it and save $500,000 a year as a result of that particular judgment.

allows, in some cases, some slight discretion to the Minister, but on the basis of the Minister's performance in the last six months when we have asked him repeatedly to explain the undertakings of a company such as Black & Decker, he totally refused. Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to set the record straight and say that we, as new Members, are perfectly free to make statements, that we were not forced to do so by any Minister, that I get along perfectly well with both Ministers
May 7, 1985

and that I am free to come or not to come to the House. I offered my services this morning because my Ministers were busy, but Hon. Members may rest assured that we are perfectly free, that we are not forced in any way to defend our Government's policy, and that we take an active part in that Government. I wanted to be on the record as having said that, and now, I would like to speak more specifically to Motion No. 2.
I think the first part of the motion, namely section (a), if 1 am not mistaken, clarifies the paragraph in question.
I even think that part of the motion would be acceptable, if the motion did not include a second part that is not acceptable to us. The first part stresses, and I am not saying it is redundant to do so, that the International Monetary Fund is to be included with the World Bank. Although I think this is covered in the preambles, the amendment does provide further clarification. However, I must reiterate that we cannot accept the amendment because it is part of a more complex motion, whose second part is totally unacceptable to us.
As for the second part, it is a firm statement of intent, the substance of which we support as well, but I think it would be dangerous at this time, to make a statement of intent that might be construed by other nations as restrictive, or which might be interpreted differently in the course of time. We have seen treaties signed after the last World War which seemed to promote freedom and which proved to be a straightjacket for some nations. I think it would be better to provide a little more latitutde with respect to the principles being laid down here, so that our representatives in these institutions can exercise, not their voting rights, which are frequently made use of at the United Nations, whose proceedings I have had a chance to observe, but their powers of persuasion, since in these organizations it is more important to establish a consensus: in other words, people analyze the problems thoroughly, discuss them and instead of submitting them immediately for a vote, they use their powers of persuasion.
So, once again, as a free agent, but not reluctant to practise my English, I prepared a short speech in response to the second part of the motion.

Canada has also been a very strong supporter of efforts over the past decade to ensure that World Bank loans promote the basic human needs of the poorest people in developing countries. In part, we have supported this approach as a means of ensuring a more equitable distribution of income in recipient countries. Moreover, we have felt that this approach would help ensure that the poor would benefit regardless of the political and ethical ideologies of the particular Government which happens to be in power at the time the loan is approved. World Bank and International Development Association loans seek to address the long-term problems of the poor, and great care should be taken before turning off programs which take a long time to get started. We are confident that the World Bank is seriously pursuing the objective of improving the
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
economic lot of the poor in recipient countries and therefore deserves our strong support.
The proposed amendment would create the erroneous impression that Canada does not believe the World Bank is pursuing these objectives. The amendment talks of Canadian initiatives and policy action in these institutions. Instead, we believe the World Bank is committed and the need is for Canada to support the effective implementation and evolution, as necessary, of existing policies.
By referring to the use of Canada's vote in these institutions, the amendment also suggests a line of action which we believe could be counter-productive. Canada has sought to avoid the use of votes in the World Bank and has encouraged decisionmaking based on consensus. As a consequence, unlike the United Nations, voting is not a common practice in these institutions. Canada, by itself, could not stop a loan and if we were to encourage other countries to exercise their votes on the executive boards, we would not be able to contain the practice to our own objectives. In other words, we would likely only encourage greater politicization of these institutions.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we want to be consistent with our policy actions, as much within international organizations as within the Canadian Government itself. We would use persuasion and even change our original concept through a document or consultations paving the way for a final decision, rather than make a hasty decision such that those basic principles might eventually be harmful to us.
Keeping in mind what I have just said, I repeat that the first part of the motion is acceptable to us, because it does shed more light even though it is not exclusive since the first part of the Bill covers everything under the Bretton Woods Acts as well as the other related organizations. However, we cannot subscribe to the first part because the second part might hamper our negotiations with respect to the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the International Finance Corporation and the International Development Association.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to this Opposition motion and especially the first part of the motion which concerns the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
First of all, I would like to point out that the approach taken by the Government to constitutional discussions on Native issues is a comprehensive one which must consider the many important interests that are at stake. The Prime Minister himself confirmed this in his preliminary remarks at the First Ministers' Conference in April. He insisted, and righly so, on the need for identifying, defining and protecting aboriginal rights, and for doing so within the Canadian Constitution. In fact, it is a process that has been going on for several years or at least several months, and at the First Ministers' Conference held by the former Government in 1984, three of the four national native people's associations made a joint proposal for negotiations leading to the application of their ancestral rights. Among these rights, the right to self-government appears to be the most important and the most fundamental one, and, in fact, the basis for successful negotiations.
The Government of Canada agrees with the native representatives that self-government will help native groups to have

May 10, 1985
Supply
more effective control over everything that concerns and affects them.
Last December, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), and the Minister of Justice, called the first federal-provincial conference held by this Government. At a meeting to prepare for the Constitutional Conference, the Government, through its spokesmen, tabled a proposal to have certain rights of these native groups recognized in the Constitution. We felt that recognition would have to involve agreement on a definition, negotiated by the governments and the groups concerned. The discussions covered the rights issue and especially the very basic issue of native self-government.
Details were worked out at two subsequent preparatory meetings for the April conference and at a number of meetings of senior officials, with the consent and support of native representatives. Generally speaking, the Government shared the view of these representatives that only a constitutional amendment could guarantee protection of ancestral rights and the establishment of a new relationship between the Native groups and the Government of Canada.
We understand the objections of the provinces to enshrining rights which they saw as being rather vague. Nevertheless, the conclusion was that without the constitutional protection or enshrinement of native rights, a special relationship between the Government, the provinces and the native peoples would not survive.
The Government, and I think this deserves some emphasis, considers this a special relationship-a relationship based on trust and honesty and the basis for future developments in the constitutional process. In his opening speech at the First Ministers' Conference last April, the Prime Minister of Canada stated, and I quote:
The Federal Government will not take any unexpected initiatives, nor will it resort to pressure tactics to make you adopt positions that run counter to your principles. We are going to play fair, with our cards on the table.
The Prime Minister went on to stress the place and rights of Native peoples and the inclusion of those rights in the Constitution. He said, and I quote the Prime Minister again:
Recognition in the Constitution of the principle of governmental autonomy would seem to be a primary objective, because it constitutes the most solemn manifestation of the establishing of an indissoluble link, a social contract, between Native peoples and governments.
Mr. Speaker, our first proposal, like the joint proposal made by the native associations, reconciled these two positions. It acknowledged in the Constitution the principle of the right of aboriginal peoples to self-government, leaving aside such issues as powers, fields of jurisdiction and financing to be negotiated later with representatives of the aboriginal peoples. Any agreement resulting from these negotiations should have the same constitutional status and provide the same protection as land claims settlement agreements.
The first proposal paved the way for the discussions I mentioned a moment ago. On every occasion the federal Government proposed a draft constitutional agreement so as to make it possible for all participants to reach agreement. This draft would have led to an amendment on self-Government as early as this year, 1985. This proposal unveiled on the eve of the First Ministers' Conference was three-fold; it included first, full recognition of the rights of aboriginal peoples to self-Government within the Canadian Federation, a point which was to be the subject of negotiated agreements; second, the willingness of the federal and provincial Governments to negotiate with representatives of the aboriginal peoples so as to conclude those agreements; and third, a specific provision stating that those special rights would be constitutionally guaranteed.
During the conference, the majority of participants came close to endorsing an amended version of that proposal in which there was no reference to the willingness or need to negotiate. It could have led to this constitutional amendment rather quickly. We have every reason to believe that we can now count on the support of seven provinces-they represent more than 50 per cent of the Canadian population-to have the amended version accepted. It has been unanimously endorsed by the Council of Native Peoples of Canada and the National Metis Association. However, two of the main groups attending the conference refrained from taking position on that issue. Just the same, the Prime Minister thought that support for the proposal ought to be reassessed at a meeting of interested Ministers to be held later on. As we know now, this meeting will take place next June 5 and 6.

It is based on the view that the divorce laws should be part of the solution rather than part of the problem in the difficult area of family relationships and family law.
It is also based on the view that once a marriage relationship has broken down irretrievably that we should sever the legal relationship with as little stress and acrimony as possible. Those are the principles that lie behind this legislation. We should stress any possibility there might be for reconciliation or mediation.
It is a fact that marriage breakdown occurs in our society. It is an unfortunate fact of life, but it is a fact. Therefore, legislation is required to settle the issues that arise once a marriage has broken down. It is the need to update and modernize our laws in this respect that leads to the introduction of this legislation.
The Divorce and Corollary Relief Bill seeks to update the 1968 Divorce Act by modifying the grounds for divorce, by improving provisions relating to support and custody and divorce procedure. The Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act will provide additional remedies to help enforce support and custody arrangements made in the case of separation or divorce.
I might mention that legislation along these lines was introduced last year by Mr. Justice MacGuigan. The divorce part of this legislation is based in large part on that with what I believe are significant improvements, taking in mind the objections and criticisms that were made last year when that Bill was initially introduced. Among the major improvements I believe will be found the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act to provide for the better enforcement of support and custody orders.
Let me deal first with the reform of the Divorce Act. That was a priority outlined in the Throne Speech of the Government. It is a priority because there is mounting pressure to modernize the law. The pressure comes from the public, the legal profession and various women's groups. The provincial governments, which are generally responsible for the administration of justice, have also urged us to proceed with divorce reform. These pressures are due to the conditions that have changed since the law was last reformed 17 years ago.
Last year in Canada there were approximately 69,000 divorces. There were 179,000 marriages. That is a ratio of 2.5 marriages for every divorce. Canada's rising divorce rate and the declining marriage rate have led some people to declare that the institution of marriage is in decline. The family is not disappearing in Canada; it is taking on new forms. People who get divorced usually wish to be remarried, to form families and carry on the family relationships.

Why should she not be able to apply for divorce immediately? This Bill provides for that. There are two ways of showing marriage breakdown under this legislation. change, by the way, from the legislation that was introduced last year.
Divorce on the basis of a fault ground provides for quicker relief from the other spouse and offers a chance to ventilate feelings, often a beneficial process. Shortening the separation period to one year from the present three years is in line with the desire to reduce the conflict between the spouses. It will also allow them to rebuild their lives more quickly. At the same time, we believe it long enough to allow for second thought and it is long enough to avoid rash and hasty divorces. If the two parties to a marriage have been living separate and apart for a year, they have not been able to patch up their differences and there is no reconciliation, the relationship has broken down and a year is certainly sufficient time to establish that. I do not think it is necessary to force people to wait another two years in addition before they can move to deal with the consequences of their marriage breakdown.
In addition, the possibility of proving marriage breakdown by fault is necessary for several reasons. First, many religious groups feel that divorce should be available immediately for moral reasons to a spouse victimized by the other. Religious beliefs and moral standards are such for certain individuals or groups that withholding a decree of divorce when it is pursued by a spouse who is the victim of adultery or cruelty would be considered immoral. For practical reasons, Mr. Speaker, we know it offers to a petitioning spouse the chance of ventilating frustrations while obtaining a judgment of divorce immediately or being granted immediate relief in the form of maintenance and or custody. That is why these grounds are being left in the legislation.
To those who favour a pure no-fault system, I answer that adultery and cruelty have long been considered valid proof of marriage breakdown and, therefore, they should stay. I can also point out that alternatives will exist and that the reduction in the separation period as an alternative means to prove marriage breakdown will render the use of fault less appealing or necessary. My guess would be that in four or five years time the use of the fault grounds will be very rare.
In addition to modifying the grounds for divorce, the principles upon which support will be provided are set out in the legislation. These do not include criteria under the present law of the conduct of the spouse. The Bill outlines the principles upon which you can obtain support. The principles do not include the conduct of the spouse. Fault is not a criteria for maintenance, nor should it be. Maintenance should be to meet the needs of a spouse, and retaining conduct as a criteria would encourage conflict between the spouses and run counter to our desire to reduce the adversarial nature of the proceedings.
In addition, this criteria has been unfairly applied in the present law. It was used to reduce maintenance received by a dependent spouse found at fault. As I mentioned before, it was never used to increase support payments owned by a supporting spouse found at fault.

The need to improve the enforcement of support and custody orders is acute, as I am sure all Members of the House know. Between one-half and three-quarters of all support orders in Canada are in arrears in whole or in part. This is an intolerable situation and is the case despite the fact that research shows that a reasonable estimate is that 80 per cent of defaulting spouses can afford to make support payments. They can afford to make them, but they choose not to. That is a situation that cannot be permitted to continue. If the House passes the legislation that is now before it, that situation will continue no longer, or at least it will not continue as easily as it has heretofore.
The wholesale flouting of custody and support orders brings the authority of the courts into disrepute. It places a tremendous emotional and financial burden on the dependent spouse and on the children of the union who have to exist without the unpaid support payments. As we know, all too often most families are forced to turn to welfare, thus placing the financial burden of the defaulters on the shoulders of the taxpayers. The estimate is that $1 billion is spent annually by governments to support custodial parents and their children. One-half of that is contributed by the federal Government under the Canada Assistance Plan. Obviously any law that permits this situation to continue would be a poor law.
In some cases, a defaulting spouse is also a missing spouse. He or she cannot be located so that a support order may be enforced. Too often children are taken by the non-custodial parent in violation of a custody order and the criminal law and they disappear beyond the reach of the parent who is supposed to have custody. In such instances, the dependent spouse or custodial parent often does not have the financial resources to trace the missing spouse or child in order to enforce the support or custody order. We all know how difficult it is to enforce these orders in a country with 10 provinces, all having different court systems and different laws. We have had to develop initiatives to improve the enforcement of such orders and these initiatives have to meet the constitutional conditions that govern us in Canada.
Canada operates under a federal system. There is one federal Government, 10 provincial Governments and two Territorial Governments. Both levels of government have their respective jurisdictions. The federal Government has jurisdiction over divorce and corollary matters to divorce, but the provinces have jurisdiction over all other incidents arising out of a marriage. Both levels of Government have an interest in
improving support and custody orders. However, the provinces are primarily responsible for the enforcement of those orders. They have the constitutional responsibility for the administration of justice and over half of such orders are made pursuant to provincial family law. They are not made as a consequence of a divorce action.
We have been consulting with the Attorneys General of the provinces to improve the enforcement of family orders. They have been very co-operative. It is with this in mind that the Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act and the Divorce and Corollary Relief Act seek to improve enforcement.
First, the Divorce Act will allow support and custody orders to be registered in any court designated by a province. That will simplify enforcement. The new Act also allows the assignment of support orders to the federal or provincial Governments so that they can enforce the orders. This is a considerable improvement. The Act will allow the courts to order a spouse both to provide security for and to pay lumpsum or periodic payments. Under the new Act, the spouse can obtain a provisional variation of a support order in the province in which he or she habitually resides and have it confirmed by a court in the province in which the erring spouse resides. That will be an advance.
The companion legislation will improve the situation pursuant to both federal and provincial laws. The Family Orders Enforcement Assistance Act will provide two new remedies for the enforcement of these matters in addition to what already exists under provincial law. The first remedy will allow the release of information from designated information banks of the federal Government in order to trace a missing spouse or child where there is a breach of a support or custody order or an access right or where a charge has been laid of child abduction in contravention of a custody order pursuant to Section 250.1 or 250.2 of the Criminal Code.
The second remedy will allow the garnishment or attachment of designated federal moneys due a support defaulter for payment to the dependent spouse or other creditor. That remedy is available to enforce a support order or a support provision of an agreement where the agreement can be enforced under provincial law by garnishment or attachment.
The federal information banks that will be opened up include designated banks of the Health and Welfare Department and the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. Mr. Speaker, parliamentarians were dismayed to see in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen that a student entrepreneur is using a life-size cardboard image of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for "photo opportunities". Right thinking Canadians will be quick to condemn this trend toward artificiality in politics, although they will, of course, acknowledge the poetic justice in that it is the Prime Minister whose presence is being so artfully simulated.
Several possible remedies for this fraudulent practice suggest themselves. Perhaps the presidential stance, or some outstanding physical characteristics, might be patented, copyrighted, or registered as a trademark to prevent counterfeiting.
In any case measures must be taken to nip this practice in the bud before it becomes too widespread. Consider the dangers. While most Canadians can probably tell the difference between the Prime Minister and a cardboard likeness, imagine the difficulties they would have if one-dimensional replicas of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) were to start springing up around the country. Dissension and dismay would spread as citizens argued over who had seen the real Member for Yukon and whether or not his lips moved.
In short, this practice could destroy by excessive exposure the images that the Government has worked so diligently to build up. It is a public menace, and must be stopped.

With the passage of this Bill, the Government will have a total of $32.2 billion of borrowing authority for the current fiscal year. I must note, however, that all borrowing authority conferred by the two Acts for this fiscal year which is unused in 1985-86 will be cancelled on March 31, 1986.
As a matter of interest to Hon. Members, I would like to outline how the Government has made use of the borrowing authority provided by Parliament for the 1984-85 fiscal year. The total amount of borrowing authority for 1984-85 was $31.9 billion. This authority consisted of $24.6 billion provided by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85; $7.3 billion provided by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85; and $7.3 billion provided by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85 (No. 2).
During the 1984-85 fiscal year, domestic borrowing operations used about $26.7 billion of borrowing authority. Of this amount, $10.4 billion was raised through the issuance of Treasury Bills, $12.5 billion through the sale of marketable bonds, and $3.8 billion through the net sale of Canada Savings Bonds. Foreign borrowing added a further $.9 billion to the use of borrowing authority. The foreign borrowing represented a 1 billion Swiss francs borrowing in the Swiss franc market in May 1984, a 120 billion yen syndicated loan in the Japanese capital market in July of 1984, and a U.S. $500 million bond issue in the Eurodollar market in March of this year.
Net standby drawings during the 1984-85 fiscal year provided $510 million of borrowing authority. There were also redemptions of foreign issues during the last fiscal year which reduced the total use of borrowing authority. These consisted of a 500 million Deutschmark private placement which matured in May 1984 and a 500 million Swiss franc private placement which matured in March 1985.
Borrowing Authority Act
As a result of these domestic and foreign financial operations, the total use of borrowing authority in the 1984-85 fiscal year was $27.6 billion, leaving $4.3 billion unused as of March 31, 1985. Of this latter amount, $2 billion was carried forward into the 1985-86 fiscal year and $2.3 billion of the authority was cancelled.
The Bill which is before us today fully meets the conditions of the understanding we reached with the Opposition Parties last December when we agreed to bring forward a request for borrowing authority for 1985-86 within two weeks of the Budget. We made that commitment at that time and are fulfilling it today. Indeed, this Bill was given its first reading less than 24 hours after the Budget was brought down.
I would like to close by asking for swift passage of this Bill for it will permit us to get on with the job. It clearly demonstrates why we need swift passage, but we do need approval for this borrowing authority. It is a very straight-forward Bill. We are only asking for borrowing authority for the balance of this year. As Hon. Members will be aware, if they have read the Budget discussion paper that was released at the time of the Budget, we are looking for a more defined parliamentary timetable surrounding the Budget process. We are hopeful that the next request for borrowing authority, which will be in respect of the 1986-87 fiscal year, will be brought down before the end of this fiscal year.
I ask Hon. Members to assist us in passing this Bill as quickly as possible to allow us to do the job that Canadians have elected us to do, the job of representing and serving the country in an efficient and responsible manner.

The tax system would no longer erode a person's purchasing power and individuals would no longer pay tax at a higher marginal rate simply because inflation boosted him or her into a higher tax bracket.
For a person on fixed income, the result of indexing was to reduce taxes each year of prices went up and leave him or her with the same real tax to pay but not the same nominal tax, which was inflation. That change put Canada on the vanguard of nations with progressive, humane tax systems. No longer were the neediest hit. No longer was the tax system claiming higher and higher shares of an individual's hard earned money simply because of inflation. That system, I believe, Sir, has served us well since it came into effect in 1974.
Last Thursday, the Minister of Finance turned back the clock and virtually wiped out one of the most progressive and humane changes in tax legislation in our history.

We Liberals know what our principles are. And since last Thursday, when this Budget was brought down, we also know what the real principles of the Conservatives are. The Conservative Government has finally shown its true face. Last Thursday's Budget has made a mockery of the Prime Minister's solemn commitments made during the election campaign.
This Budget is a betrayal of the trust of Canadians. The Minister has deceived the Canadian people.
This Budget is a direct attack against Canadian men and women on low incomes who are being hit by a whole series of tax increases. A real downpour, as the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) said. "Taxes, taxes, taxes!" to use the words of the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien). The tax on gas: 2 cents more per litre. The Government is going to use the money to pay the oil multinationals the $2 billion it agreed to pay them under the Western Oil Accord.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) promised the House that this measure would not result in any tax increases for Canadians. We have been deceived. This Budget contains a whole list, a series, an avalanche, a veritable downpour of taxes: federal sales tax exemptions on certain products have been withdrawn; a 1 per cent increase in federal sales tax; a 25-cent increase in excise tax on a large package of cigarettes; a 2 per cent increase in the excise tax on alcohol. Even candy is being taxed! This is a cruel Budget, a cowardly Budget!
It is also a regressive Budget. It hits those least able to pay. It hits the consumer. There is a 1 per cent hike in the federal sales tax to 11 per cent. New items not previously taxed have been added-everything from children's candies and soft drinks to pet foods and alternative energy equipment. The 11 per cent tax now applies to health care products as well, such as bandages. Scrapes and bruises are suddenly taxable items, as well as soap and shampoo. It will cost more to stay clean. It really is a dirty Budget.
In 1982, the average family of four in the under $20,000 income range spent $372.60 per year on health care products. The Minister has just raised that bill by $41, 11 per cent, to $413.60. Again it is a tax which will hurt those who can afford it least. They will be the hardest hit. Most important is that the 11 per cent sales tax now applies to surgical supplies in doctors' offices, dental instruments, X-ray apparatus and X-ray film. A trip to the dentist will be more expensive, especially if one has children. These increases are expected to cost the health field alone some $75 million per year in additional costs to average Canadians going to a dictor or going to a dentist.

That is right. I must have hit a nerve because suddenly Conservative Members are interjecting. It will take a few months for old age pensioners to realize what is happening. They will know what has happened when they go to the supermarket to do their shopping and find that the price of groceries-meat, milk, cheese, everything-has risen, and when they receive their pension cheques and discover that they are not receiving the kinds of increases they used to get until now. Each and every one of them will know what has happened because they can clearly see what has happened.
A large percentage of our old age pensioners, particularly single women, widows, those who have never been married, and those who stayed home while they were married bringing up their children and who have certainly not worked in recent years, are living in poverty now, It is a sad fact that we really do not know how they live. I see that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) is here in the Chamber, Mr. Speaker. Since Parliament will not be sitting in July, I invite the Hon. Member to spend a half a day with me to visit some of the soup kitchens operating in our great City of Winnipeg. Let us go to the soup kitchen off Broadway which is operating in the Broadway Optimist Building. Let us visit the Salvation Army and some of the native centres which are feeding people. Let us visit those Catholic churches which are handing out parcels of food, groceries and canned goods. Let us talk to the people at these centres. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine and I could urge the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) to do the same type of thing in Toronto. It will be seen that there are hundreds of thousands of people in this wealthy country who are living in conditions akin to the way people live in the Third World.
In Winnipeg, we have a successful school nutrition program in place. When it was first started, many people said it was not necessary. It was said that this was not the responsibility of the schools. There are young people in Winnipeg whose one and only nutritious meal a day comes from the school. I say that is a disgrace. It is a disgrace to every Canadian. It is a disgrace to every Member of Parliament that this type of situation can exist in our country.
I say to the Members of the Conservative Party: Go out and look at what is happening. Go out and see how people are living. If those Members have any kind of heart, they will say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), "You are moving in the wrong direction." We cannot, in all conscience, permit so many people to continue in the way they are living, not if we have any shred of compassion, any shred of decency.
I would like to deal with what the Budget means for
children. What we have in place is a clearly regressive plan. By
the very calculations of the Minister of Finance, there will be a withdrawal of some $15 million from families in the period 1985-86 and some $40 million in the period 1986-87 because of cut-backs in the family allowance program. These family allowances are being cut back because we are abandoning their indexation. In fact, the purchasing power of that money has lost one-third of what it could buy 10 years ago. The child tax exemption is being significantly reduced through this Budget. The child tax credit has been significantly altered through a reduced income threshold for qualifiers and through reduced indexing.
I would now like to deal with poverty in families. According to the report to which I referred earlier, the poverty rate for a family with one child increased by 17.2 per cent from 1980 to 1983. The poverty rate for a family with two children increased by 25.7 per cent from 1980 to 1983. The poverty rate for a family with three or more children increased by 33 per cent from 1980 to 1983. These are shocking figures. I urge the Government to consider the real situation and increase the disposable income of people in low income brackets instead of decreasing it, as has been done through the proposals in the Budget.
I suggest we should not be thinking about increasing regressive sales taxes on essentials. We should be removing these taxes. We should be removing the sales tax from the important and necessary items required by all families. We should not be increasing these taxes. In conclusion, I say again that this Budget is probably the worst I have ever had to deal with in my more than 20 years in Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly to Motion No. 27. As the Indian Act now reads, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) has complete discretion in Subsection 17(1) to constitute new bands from existing band lists, in effect to split bands. In Subsection 17(2) he also has discretion to divide reserve lands and funds accordingly. Bill C-31 originally provided for future band splits to require approval of a majority of band electors.
In reviewing the Bill, however, it became clear that this approach would indeed be impractical. In fact, it might even make band splits impossible. This is because such splits normally involve a minority group, frequently one that lives apart from the majority of the band. There may be good reasons for acting on the desire of such minorities to split away, but it is unlikely that a majority of the whole band would agree.
During the standing committee's clause by clause review, the Bill was revised to require that those persons proposing to form a new band make a request to the Minister, rather than that a majority of all band electors approve. Any split would still be subject to the Minister's discretion, so inappropriate cases can be rejected. If a decision is taken to split a band, it is only logical to split the band's land and resources accordingly. The members of the new band obviously have a right to a fair share of the assets of the whole band. It would be inconsistent to give a group within a band a right to request the Minister to constitute a new band without also giving them effective access to a reasonable portion of band assets.
The present motion does not seek to amend Subsection 17(1) as reported by the standing committee. To be consistent, and indeed in fairness to those who may seek to form a new band, we cannot accept the change proposed in this motion to Subsection 17(2). In fact, probably the fairest way to share band assets in the case of band splits would be to leave the matter to an independent third party, namely the Minister. Such decisions would only be taken after consultation with all those affected. I might also point out, Mr. Speaker, that we are not talking about a frequent problem. In the past 10 years, for example, there have only been approximately two dozen cases of band splits under Subsection 17(1).
In conclusion, I urge all Members to vote to defeat this motion. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
